title: Shared state and testing coroutines
goal: By the end you can protect shared state across coroutines with atomics or a Mutex, explain why limitedParallelism(1) is not a lock, and test timing-heavy code such as retry with backoff on virtual time with runTest, test dispatchers and backgroundScope.

warmup.q: 100 coroutines on a `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` view each run `val b = balance; val c = fx.convert(1); balance = b + c`, where `fx.convert` is a suspend call to the FX service. Each credit adds 1. What is `balance` at the end?
options: Exactly 100, because only one coroutine runs at a time on the view
Usually far less than 100, because the coroutines interleave at fx.convert
Exactly 100, but only if fx.convert doesn't suspend for long
The code fails, because a one-thread view rejects concurrent coroutines
warmup.why: A one-thread view runs one coroutine at a time only between suspension points. When a credit suspends in `fx.convert`, the thread is free and the next credit reads the same old balance. When they resume, each writes its own `b + c` over the others. The KDoc's own heading for this is "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!".

sections.h: Coroutines on Default race like threads, and the same tools fix them

try.title: Count a million payments five ways
steps: Read `SharedCounter.kt`. 100 coroutines on Default each count 10,000 payments. Predict which counters reach 1,000,000, and which is slowest.
Run the Java twin, which uses 8 threads and a `ReentrantLock`.

code.title: SharedCounter.kt
code.src:
package workbench.coroutines.l10

import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope
import kotlinx.coroutines.launch
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong
import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis

private var plain = 0L
@Volatile private var volatileCount = 0L

/** 100 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default each count 10,000 captured payments. */
suspend fun count(label: String, increment: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit, read: () -> Long) {
    val ms = measureTimeMillis {
        coroutineScope { repeat(100) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(10_000) { increment() } } } }
    }
    println("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms".format(label, read(), ms))
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    count("plain var", { plain++ }, { plain })
    count("@Volatile var", { volatileCount++ }, { volatileCount })
    val atomic = AtomicLong()
    count("AtomicLong", { atomic.incrementAndGet() }, { atomic.get() })
    val mutex = Mutex()
    var guarded = 0L
    count("Mutex.withLock", { mutex.withLock { guarded++ } }, { guarded })
    val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)
    var onOneThread = 0L
    count("withContext(limited(1))", { withContext(confined) { onOneThread++ } }, { onOneThread })
}

alt.title: SharedCounterJava.java

try.expect: The plain and `@Volatile` counters come out short, by a different amount each run. `AtomicLong`, `Mutex.withLock` and the one-thread view all reach exactly 1,000,000. `AtomicLong` is fastest by far; the `Mutex` and the `withContext` switch for every increment take about a second, because each increment pays for a lock or a dispatch. The Java twin shows the same split, with `ReentrantLock` much cheaper than a Mutex here because these threads never suspend.

sections.h: A one-thread view is not a mutex
sections.body:
A view such as `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` runs at most one of its coroutines at a time. That looks like a lock, and the KDoc has a heading of its own to say it isn't one: "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!"

The view guarantees that code **between suspension points** runs one coroutine at a time, with a happens-before edge from each to the next, so `counter++` on it is safe. But the moment a coroutine suspends, the view's thread is free and the next coroutine runs. Any sequence that suspends in the middle is open to interleaving:

```kotlin
withContext(oneAtATime) {
    val before = balances[account] ?: 0L
    val cents = fx.toEurCents(amount, currency)    // suspends: another credit runs here
    balances[account] = before + cents             // writes over the other credit
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: one thread, but an async step in the middle
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L), oneThread)
    .thenCombine(fx.toEurCentsAsync(amount, currency), Long::sum)        // another credit runs meanwhile
    .thenAcceptAsync(after -> balances.put(account, after), oneThread);  // writes over the other credit
```

Play it out in the simulator: two credits, one thread, and a suspension in the middle of each. (The simulator lets you switch after any line. On the real view a switch can only happen at the suspending line, and that is enough to lose a credit.)

There are two fixes. Move the suspension out of the critical part: convert first, then do the read and the write with nothing that suspends between them. On a one-thread view that is now safe, because nothing else can run in the middle. Or hold a `Mutex` across the whole sequence, which keeps other credits out even while the holder is suspended. The first is faster, because the conversions overlap. Use the second when the suspending call really must sit inside, for example a ledger check whose answer must not go stale before you write.

The general rule is the one you learned for threads. A critical section is safe only if nothing else can run in the middle of it. For coroutines, "in the middle" means any suspension point, including the ones hidden inside functions you call.

sim.title: Two credits on limitedParallelism(1)
sim.intro: Both credits run on a one-thread view, so only one runs at a time. But each one gives the thread away when it suspends in fx.toEurCents. You are the scheduler: click a credit to run its next line. Can you end with balance = 100 after two credits of 100?

steps.code: val cents = fx.toEurCents(1, "EUR")   // suspends: the thread is free
val cents = fx.toEurCents(1, "EUR")   // suspends: the thread is free

goal.say: Lost credit. Both read 0 before either wrote. One coroutine at a time between suspensions is not one credit at a time.

try.title: Interleave three credits, then lock them
steps: Read `NotAMutex.kt`. Predict the order of the `read` and `write` lines for the one-thread view, then for the `Mutex`.
Look at the last part: why does the nested `withLock` time out instead of returning `inner`?
Run the Java twin, where a single-thread executor interleaves the same way and `ReentrantLock` happily locks twice.

code.title: NotAMutex.kt

alt.title: NotAMutexJava.java

try.expect: On the one-thread view, all three `read balance` lines print before any `write balance`: each credit suspended in the middle and let the next one in. With the `Mutex`, each credit reads and writes before the next one starts. The nested `withLock` times out after 500 ms, because a Mutex is not reentrant: the inner lock waits for the outer one, which waits for the inner one. The Java twin interleaves the same way on one thread, and its `ReentrantLock` reports a hold count of 2.

steps: Read `VirtualTime.kt`. It calls `runTest` from a plain `main`. Predict the virtual time of each log line, and how much real time the first `runTest` takes.
Look at the last line: why did the clock stay at 0 while a real second went by?

code.title: VirtualTime.kt

try.expect: The lines print at virtual 1,000, 1,200, 3,000, 3,200 and 3,500 ms, in that order, and `await returned` at 3,500. The real time stays well under a second, and most of it is the test library starting up. The last `runTest` reports virtual 0 ms and about 1,000 real ms: `withContext(Dispatchers.Default)` left the test scheduler, so its `delay` was a real one.

sections.h: Standard or Unconfined, and backgroundScope for work that never ends
sections.body:
`runTest` uses a `StandardTestDispatcher` by default. With it, `launch` only queues the new coroutine, and nothing runs until the test body suspends or advances the scheduler. Tests stay predictable, because you decide when each child runs. Production dispatchers don't run a child immediately either, so this is also the more honest default.

`UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` enters a new coroutine at once and runs it to its first suspension, like `Dispatchers.Unconfined`. That is handy for a collector that must be subscribed before the next line emits, such as a test of a SharedFlow with no replay:

```kotlin
backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) {
    tracker.transitions.collect { seen += it }    // subscribed before the next line runs
}
tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED)
```

```java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes first, then runs the action that emits
StepVerifier.create(tracker.transitions())
    .then(() -> tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED))
    .expectNextMatches(t -> t.to() == PaymentStatus.CAPTURED)
    .thenCancel()
    .verify();
```

If you mix dispatchers, give them all the same `testScheduler`. Two schedulers mean two clocks, and one of them will not move.

`backgroundScope` is for coroutines that never finish on their own: a poller, a collector of a StateFlow, the sharing scope of a `stateIn`. `runTest` waits for every child before it returns, so an endless child in the test scope itself would hang until the 60-second timeout. Coroutines in `backgroundScope` are cancelled when the test body ends instead. Two details matter. `advanceUntilIdle()` stops once only background work is left (otherwise a poller would keep it busy forever), so drive background work with `advanceTimeBy`. And a failure in `backgroundScope` doesn't stop the test at once, but it is reported when the test ends, so the test still fails.

This lesson's lab is written the way these rules suggest. The retry tests read `currentTime` to check each wait exactly, and the balance tests count how many conversions overlap instead of timing them. On the stub, one of those tests reports 0 virtual milliseconds: the stub's conversions ran on a real `Default` thread, outside the virtual clock.

For flows there is also Turbine (`app.cash.turbine`, not on this lab's classpath), which adds `flow.test { awaitItem() }`. Its waits use a 3-second wall-clock timeout, not the virtual clock.

try.title: Watch the two test dispatchers and a background poller
steps: Read `TestDispatchers.kt`. Predict the order in each of the two lists, and the poll count after each line.
Move the poller from `backgroundScope.launch` to a plain `launch`, and add `runTest(timeout = 3.seconds)` (import `kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds`). Predict, then run.

code.title: TestDispatchers.kt

try.expect: `StandardTestDispatcher: [after launch, child ran]` and `UnconfinedTestDispatcher: [child ran, after launch]`. The poller has run 5 times after `advanceTimeBy(5_500)`, and still 5 after `advanceUntilIdle()`, which ignores background work. After your change, `advanceUntilIdle()` treats the poller as foreground work and runs it again and again, millions of virtual seconds' worth, until the 3-second wall-clock timeout stops everything with `UncompletedCoroutinesError` (an `AssertionError`): the test body did not run to completion.

analogy: Shared state is the cash drawer at a shop. An atomic is a till that adds a sale in one press of a key. A `Mutex` is the key to the drawer: whoever holds it counts, takes and writes down, and the others wait their turn, without standing around blocking the aisle (they suspend). A one-thread view is a rule that only one cashier stands at the till at a time. That rule doesn't stop a cashier from walking off to phone the bank in the middle of counting, letting the next cashier count the same drawer. `runTest` is a rehearsal with a stage clock that jumps straight to the next cue, so a day of trading takes seconds. The analogy breaks on reentry: a shopkeeper holding the drawer key can open the drawer twice. A coroutine holding a Mutex that asks for it again waits for itself forever.
in_your_world: Most payment state lives in Oracle, where row locks and unique keys do this job, but services keep some state in memory: per-merchant rate-limit counters, a cache of FX rates, the in-flight totals of a settlement run. Counters belong in atomics. A compound update, such as checking a merchant's daily limit and then reserving the amount, needs a `Mutex` held across the check and the reservation, with any suspending call (the FX conversion, the fraud score) done before the lock if you can. Don't reach for `limitedParallelism(1)` as a lock: it serializes code only between suspension points. For tests, inject dispatchers everywhere (Quarkus beans can take a `CoroutineDispatcher` from a producer method), so a test passes `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` and a retry policy with a 30-second cap tests in milliseconds.
mistake: The most common mistake is protecting a sequence that suspends in the middle with something that only works between suspensions: a `limitedParallelism(1)` view, a single-threaded dispatcher, or `synchronized` around code that was refactored into a suspend function. It passes code review because it reads like a lock, and it passes tests that never make two coroutines overlap. Under load, two credits read the same balance, both suspend in the FX call, and one overwrites the other. The fix is to look for every suspension point inside the critical section. Move it out (compute first, then read and write with nothing in between), or hold a `Mutex` across the whole sequence and keep that sequence short.

compare.title: A merchant limit check: ReentrantLock vs Mutex

java.title: DailyLimits.java

kotlin.title: DailyLimits.kt

compare.note: The shape is identical: do the slow call first, then check and reserve under one lock. Two things differ. Waiting for a `ReentrantLock` blocks a thread, while waiting for a `Mutex` suspends a coroutine, so a burst of 5,000 reservations doesn't need 5,000 threads. And the Java lock is reentrant while the Mutex isn't, so a helper that takes the Mutex again from inside `withLock` hangs instead of nesting. The Kotlin version has one extra trap that Java can't have: if someone later moves `fraud.score` inside `withLock`, it still works but holds the lock across a network call, and if they replace the Mutex with a one-thread dispatcher, it stops being correct at all.

worked.title: Test a retry policy without waiting for it

steps.say: A capture client retries the issuer on `IOException`: up to 5 attempts, waits starting at 200 ms, doubling, capped at 2 s. The existing test uses real time and `Thread.sleep`. It takes 3 seconds, and it fails on CI about once a week.
Move to `runTest`. The waits are `delay` calls on the test dispatcher, so they become virtual, and the test can check each attempt's exact virtual time instead of a window.

The test went back to real time when someone added `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` around the HTTP call inside the client: its `delay` calls now ran on IO. Inject the dispatcher, and give the test the test scheduler's one.
Add the case people forget: cancellation during a wait must stop the retries. Virtual time lets you stop exactly between two attempts.

Self-check: suppose the helper wrapped both the attempt and the `delay` in one `runCatching` and retried on any failure. What would the cancel test report? (`calls` would be 5, not 2. After the cancel, each `delay` throws at once, `runCatching` swallows it as a failed attempt, and the loop races through the remaining attempts. The test catches it because it counts calls instead of timing them. Lesson 5 of this track showed the same trap.)

lab.title: Fix a balance book, then write retry with backoff
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. Read `SharedStateAndTestingTest.kt` first: it is the spec, and every test runs on virtual time.
In `BalanceBook.credit`, call `fx.toEurCents` first, outside any lock. Then do the read and the write inside `mutex.withLock { }`. Replace the one-thread view with a `Mutex` in `balance` too.

Write `retryWithBackoff`. Loop over attempts 1 to `times - 1`: return the block's result on success; on an exception, rethrow `CancellationException`, rethrow when `retryOn` is false, otherwise `delay` and grow the wait. Then make the last attempt outside the loop, so its exception reaches the caller.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: On the stub, `100 concurrent credits all land` reports 100 cents instead of 10,000: every credit read 0 before any wrote. The second test reports 0 virtual ms because the stub's conversions ran on a real `Default` thread, outside the test clock.
Catch `CancellationException` before `Exception`, and rethrow it. `kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException` is the class to import.
The cancel test cancels the job during a `delay`. A `delay` that is not inside your `try` simply throws, and the loop ends without another attempt.

drill.title: A safe counter map and a virtual-time test, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `class MerchantCounts` with `suspend fun record(merchant: String)` that calls a suspending `fraud.check(merchant)` first, then increments that merchant's count, safe for many coroutines on `Dispatchers.Default`. Then write a `runTest` test that checks a function `pollEvery(1.seconds)` has polled 3 times after 3.5 virtual seconds, using `backgroundScope` for the endless poller.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: Coroutines on `Dispatchers.Default` race like threads. `@Volatile` doesn't make `count++` safe; atomics do, for single values.
A `Mutex` protects a sequence of steps. `withLock` suspends instead of blocking, and the Mutex is fair and not reentrant: locking it again from inside hangs.
`limitedParallelism(1)` serializes code only between suspension points, so a read, a suspending call and a write on it can lose updates. Move the suspension out, or hold a Mutex.
`runTest` skips `delay` with a virtual clock (`currentTime`, `advanceTimeBy`, `runCurrent`, `advanceUntilIdle`). Delays on real dispatchers stay real, so inject dispatchers.
`StandardTestDispatcher` (the default) queues new coroutines; `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` starts them at once. Share one `testScheduler` between them.
Put never-ending coroutines in `backgroundScope`. `advanceUntilIdle` ignores them, and `runTest` cancels them at the end.

quiz.q: A merchant limit check runs `mutex.withLock { if (spent + amount <= limit) { reserve(amount) } }`, and `reserve` itself calls `mutex.withLock { spent += amount }`. What happens on the first reservation?
options: It works: a coroutine may take a lock it already holds
It throws `IllegalStateException`: the mutex is already locked
It hangs: the inner `withLock` waits for the outer one, which never finishes
The inner `withLock` is skipped, so `spent` never changes
quiz.why: `Mutex` is not reentrant. The inner `withLock` suspends until the lock is free, but the lock is held by the same code waiting on it, so it never is. Take the lock once at the top and have `reserve` assume it is held.

quiz.q: Which tool fits a per-merchant counter of approved payments, incremented by many coroutines on Default, where each update is just "add one"?
options: A `ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong>` and `incrementAndGet()`
A `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` view around the whole handler
A `Mutex` held across the handler's network calls
`@Volatile` on the map field
quiz.why: Each update is one atomic step on one value, so an atomic is the cheapest correct tool: it never suspends or blocks. A Mutex held across network calls serializes everything, and `@Volatile` on the field only covers the reference to the map, not the increments.

quiz.q: Inside `runTest`, the code under test calls `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(2_000) }`. What does the test see?
options: `currentTime` jumps by 2,000 and the test finishes at once
The test fails at once, because `Dispatchers.IO` is forbidden in `runTest`
`currentTime` jumps by 2,000, but only after `advanceUntilIdle()`
The test waits about 2 real seconds, and `currentTime` doesn't move
quiz.why: Only delays on the test dispatcher are virtual. `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` leaves the test scheduler, so that `delay` is a real one, invisible to the virtual clock. Inject the dispatcher so the test can pass `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)`.

quiz.q: A test launches `launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); poll() } }` in the `runTest` body, checks the poll count after `advanceTimeBy(3_500)`, and ends. What happens?
options: The test passes; the loop is cancelled when the body ends
The test hangs until the `runTest` timeout, because `runTest` waits for every child
The loop never runs, because `launch` only queues it
`advanceTimeBy` throws, because the loop never ends
quiz.why: `runTest` waits for all children of the test scope before it returns, and this one never ends, so the test fails after the wall-clock timeout (60 s by default). Launch endless work in `backgroundScope`, which `runTest` cancels when the body ends.

quiz.q: From lesson 5 of this track: a retry helper wraps each attempt in `runCatching { block() }` and retries on any failure. The caller is cancelled while an attempt is suspended in an HTTP call. What happens?
options: The `CancellationException` counts as a failed attempt, and the helper goes on to the next one
The retries stop at once, because `runCatching` never catches `CancellationException`
The coroutine is killed and no `finally` blocks run
The helper waits for the HTTP call to finish, then stops
quiz.why: `runCatching` catches every `Throwable`, including `CancellationException`, so the cancel is logged and handled as a failed attempt. If the backoff `delay` sits outside the `runCatching`, it throws at once and ends the loop more or less by luck; if it sits inside, the loop races through every remaining attempt. Rethrow `CancellationException` before treating anything as retryable.

flashcards.front: Does `@Volatile` make `count++` safe across coroutines on `Dispatchers.Default`?
flashcards.back: No. It makes each read and write visible, but `count++` is still read, add, write. Use an atomic or a `Mutex`.

flashcards.front: What does `Mutex.withLock` do while another coroutine holds the lock?
flashcards.back: It suspends the caller (no thread is blocked) until the lock is free, and the Mutex hands out the lock in arrival order.

flashcards.front: A coroutine holding a `Mutex` calls `withLock` on it again. What happens?
flashcards.back: It suspends forever: `Mutex` is not reentrant.
It runs one coroutine at a time only between suspension points. When one suspends, another runs, so a sequence with a suspension in the middle can interleave.
It is skipped: the virtual clock (`currentTime`) jumps forward by 1,000 ms, keeping the order of events.
Standard queues the new coroutine until the test yields or advances time. Unconfined starts it at once and runs it to its first suspension.

flashcards.front: Where do never-ending coroutines go in a `runTest` test?
flashcards.back: `backgroundScope`: they are cancelled when the test body ends, and `advanceUntilIdle()` doesn't wait for them.

terms.plain: A coroutine lock: waiting suspends instead of blocking. Fair, and not reentrant.
Code that must run without anything else touching the same state in the middle of it.
Keeping mutable state reachable from only one coroutine or thread, so it needs no lock.
The test scheduler's clock. Delays advance it instantly instead of waiting.
The scope runTest runs the test body in, with currentTime and a test dispatcher.
A test dispatcher that queues tasks until the test lets the scheduler run.
A scope inside runTest for endless work; it is cancelled when the test body ends.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate replaced a `Mutex` with `Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)` in the merchant limit check "because it's simpler and only one coroutine runs at a time anyway". The check calls the fraud service between reading and writing the limit. Explain what can go wrong, and how you'd test it without real time.
explain_back.answer: The one-thread view only guarantees one coroutine at a time between suspension points. The fraud call suspends, so while one check waits for the fraud service, the thread runs the next check, which reads the same "spent so far" value. Both then pass the limit check and both reserve, so a merchant can go over its limit. A Mutex held across the whole check keeps the second one out even while the first is suspended; better still, call the fraud service first and then do the read and the reservation together under the lock, with nothing suspending in between. To test it, I'd use runTest with a fake fraud service that just calls delay(50), launch a hundred reservations, and assert on the totals and on how many overlapped. On virtual time that is deterministic and runs in milliseconds, as long as the class takes its dispatcher as a parameter instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.Default.

deeper.body:
`Semaphore(permits)` in `kotlinx.coroutines.sync` is the counting version of a Mutex: `withPermit { }` lets at most n coroutines in at once. It is the coroutine counterpart of the shared `Semaphore` from lesson 3 of the virtual threads track, and like the Mutex it suspends rather than blocks. Since 1.9 you can no longer cast a `Mutex` to a `Semaphore`; they are separate types.

`Mutex` has an optional owner: `lock(owner)` and `withLock(owner)` record who holds it, and `holdsLock(owner)` checks it. Passing an owner turns a reentrant call into an immediate `IllegalStateException` instead of a silent hang, which is a cheap safety net in code where a helper might be called with the lock held.

The test library has more knobs than this lesson uses. Several `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler, name = ...)` instances can share one scheduler, so production code that takes two dispatchers (IO and CPU) can get two named test dispatchers with one clock. `Dispatchers.setMain(...)` and `resetMain()` swap the Main dispatcher for UI-style code. And `runTest` reports uncaught exceptions from coroutines it doesn't own at the end of the test, through a `ServiceLoader` hook, which is why a forgotten `GlobalScope.launch` that throws can fail an unrelated test.

Finally, virtual time is not a load test. It proves that the order and the timing logic are right. It says nothing about how long the real FX service takes, how a real Mutex behaves with 5,000 waiters, or whether Oracle keeps up. Keep a few real-time integration tests, with generous margins, for that.
